passage:
Monday: Jomon, fifteen, got a message on a gaming chat from someone called "Riya" who said she was sixteen and lived nearby. She was funny and knew all his favourite players. Jomon felt flattered.

Thursday: "Riya" asked for a photo, then a more private one. When he said no, the tone changed: "Send it or I'll tell everyone what you said." Jomon's hands went cold. He didn't sleep. He almost sent it just to make it stop.

Saturday: He told his older sister Tanuja, shaking. She didn't shout. She helped him take screenshots, block the account and report it. Then they told their parents together, who went with him to the cyber cell. Jomon cried with relief when the officer said, "You did the right thing."

qa.q: Who did Jomon tell on Saturday?
qa.a: He told his older sister Tanuja.

qa.q: Why did Jomon almost send the photo?
qa.a: He was frightened by the threat and exhausted from not sleeping, so giving in felt like the only way to make the pressure stop.

qa.q: What made Tanuja's response helpful?
qa.a: She stayed calm, helped him keep screenshots, block and report the account, and brought in their parents, so he wasn't facing it alone.

qa.q: What would change if Jomon had kept the threat secret?
qa.a: The person could have kept pressuring him, and he would have carried the fear alone without the protection of his family and the police.

grounding: It shows a teen recognising manipulative online contact that turns into blackmail, and reporting it to trusted adults.

passage: Neelam, listen, this happened to my friend Minakshi's son when you were small. A man online said he was a talent scout. He told the boy he could be in advertisements, that he just needed to pay a registration fee and send photos. The boy was so happy he didn't tell anyone. The man kept asking for more money, and then said, "If you tell your parents, the offer is cancelled." That line is what made Minakshi's son stop and think. Why would a real job need secrets? He showed his mother the chat. She called the helpline, and they learned it was a known trick. The money was gone, but the boy was safe. Remember that: real people don't ask you to hide things from your family.

qa.q: What did the man say he was?
qa.a: He said he was a talent scout.

qa.q: What made Minakshi's son suspicious in the end?
qa.a: The demand to keep it secret from his parents made him wonder why a genuine offer would need hiding, so doubt replaced his excitement.

qa.q: What should Neelam do if an online contact asks for secrets to be kept?
qa.a: Neelam should treat it as a warning sign, stop replying, keep the messages and tell a parent or trusted adult straight away.

qa.q: How might Minakshi have felt when her son showed her the chat?
qa.a: She was probably shaken that he'd been targeted but relieved he came to her, and glad to act quickly with the helpline. 🙏

grounding: An elder uses a family memory to teach a younger person to recognise a fraud's demand for secrecy and to tell trusted adults.

passage: Deepak had forty minutes before his bus to the coaching centre when the message arrived: "Your account will be blocked today. Click here to verify your bank details." It had his name and the bank's logo. His father's card was linked to Deepak's phone for fees, and panic rose in his chest. He was about to tap the link when his friend Yusuf, waiting with him at the bus stop, leaned over. "Bro, look at the sender. It's a random number." Deepak's thumb froze. "But it says today." "That's the trick. They rush you." Deepak didn't click. He called his father, who checked with the bank from his office. The message was fake. His father reported the number and thanked Yusuf by name that evening.

qa.q: How long did Deepak have before his bus?
qa.a: He had forty minutes.

qa.q: Why did panic rise in Deepak's chest?
qa.a: The message used his name, the logo and a same-day deadline, and his father's card was linked to his phone, so he feared causing a real problem.

qa.q: What is the wise step Deepak took instead of clicking?
qa.a: He called his father so an adult could check directly with the bank, rather than acting on the rushed message.

qa.q: How does Yusuf see the urgent message?
qa.a: Yusuf sees the random sender and the "today" deadline as signs of a trick designed to rush people into acting without thinking.

grounding: It shows a teen under time pressure recognising a phishing scam and turning to a trusted adult.

passage: For two weeks, someone called 'Rhea' had been messaging Arnab, fifteen, on a gaming chat: compliments, music, jokes about their Kolkata school. Then, one night in his room in their Salt Lake flat, the tone changed. 'Send 5,000 by tomorrow or I'll send our chats, edited, to your whole class.' Arnab's hands went cold. He hadn't done anything wrong, but edited chats could look like anything. He almost opened his savings app. Instead, heart pounding, he knocked on his sister Kalyani's door. She read it once. 'Don't pay. Don't reply. Screenshot everything.' They woke their parents together. That night Baba helped Arnab report the account on the platform and on the government cybercrime portal. Arnab barely slept, but for the first time in hours, he could breathe.

qa.q: What did 'Rhea' threaten to do if Arnab didn't pay?
qa.a: Send edited versions of their chats to his whole class.

qa.q: What was Arnab feeling when the threat arrived?
qa.a: He was frightened and panicked, with cold hands, worried that edited chats could make him look bad.

qa.q: Why were Kalyani's instructions the right ones?
qa.a: Not paying or replying stops giving the blackmailer power, and screenshots keep evidence for reporting.

qa.q: How might it feel for Arnab's parents to be woken with this news?
qa.a: They would likely be shaken but relieved he came to them before paying anything.

grounding: Shows a teen recognising blackmail through online contact and reporting it to trusted adults.

passage: 'Kashish di, look, a modelling scout messaged me!' Avni held out her phone across the kitchen table. 'He says I have the face for ads.' Kashish read it. 'He wants more photos, “casual ones”, and wants you to keep it secret from your parents till the contract?' 'He said it's normal. Surprise for them.' 'Hmm. Does a real agency ask a fourteen-year-old to hide things from her parents?' Avni hesitated. 'I guess not.' 'And why's he in a hurry? “Reply tonight or the chance is gone.”' 'That's weird too.' 'Secret, hurry, photos. Three red flags.' Avni went quiet. 'I already sent one selfie.' 'That's okay. It's not your fault, and you did right to tell me. Let's block, report, and tell Mami together, right now.' Avni nodded, a little shaky.

qa.q: What did the 'scout' ask Avni to keep secret?
qa.a: He asked her to keep it secret from her parents until the contract.

qa.q: Why did Avni go quiet after Kashish named the three red flags?
qa.a: She was realising the message was not a real opportunity and worried because she had already sent one selfie.

qa.q: How did Kashish respond helpfully when Avni admitted sending a selfie?
qa.a: She stayed calm, told Avni it was not her fault, and turned straight to blocking, reporting and telling Mami together that same day.

qa.q: What would change if Avni had kept the chat secret as asked?
qa.a: She would have faced the pressure alone, making it easier for him to push for more photos.

grounding: Shows a teen recognising grooming tactics online and reporting with a trusted adult.

passage:
For three weeks, someone called Rhea messaged me on a game chat. She was funny, liked the same music, said I was mature for sixteen. I'm Kamal. I felt special.
Then she asked for a private photo. I said no. She sent back a photo of me from my profile with a message: Send what I asked, or I'll edit this and share it with your whole school.
My hands went cold. I didn't reply. I didn't delete anything either, because I remembered a talk at school: keep evidence.
I told my aunt Rehana that evening. She didn't get angry at me. She said, “This is not your fault. You did the right thing.” She helped me take screenshots, block the account and report it to the cyber-crime portal that same night.

qa.q: What did Rhea threaten to do?
qa.a: To edit the photo and share it with the whole school.

qa.q: How did Kamal feel when the threat arrived?
qa.a: Kamal felt frightened and panicked, with cold hands, after first feeling special.

qa.q: What steps did Kamal and Rehana take, and why were they right?
qa.a: Kamal didn't reply or send anything, kept evidence and told Rehana, who blocked, reported and supported Kamal the same night.

qa.q: How did Rehana respond when Kamal told her?
qa.a: She stayed calm, said it was not Kamal's fault, and helped report the account that same night.

grounding: A teenager recognises an online blackmail attempt and tells a trusted adult, who reports it the same day.

passage:
Counsellor's note. Usha Menon.
Lalit (fifteen) came to me this morning, very anxious. Last night he got a message saying he'd won a new phone in a lucky draw. To claim it, he had to pay a small delivery fee through a link. He had already typed in his mother's card details but hadn't pressed pay.
He kept saying, “I'm so stupid.” I told him he was not stupid; these messages are designed to trick people, and he did well to stop and tell someone.
We called his mother together. She contacted her bank at once and blocked the card. We reported the message on the national cyber-crime helpline.
Next step: a short talk for Class 10 on lucky-draw scams.

qa.q: What did the message say Lalit had won?
qa.a: A new phone in a lucky draw.

qa.q: How was Lalit feeling when he came to the counsellor?
qa.a: He was very anxious and ashamed, calling himself stupid.

qa.q: What steps did the counsellor take to protect Lalit and his family?
qa.a: She reassured him, called his mother, who blocked the card with the bank, and reported the scam on the helpline.

qa.q: How might Lalit's mother feel when she gets the call?
qa.a: She may be alarmed but relieved that Lalit stopped and told an adult before paying.

grounding: A counsellor helps a fifteen-year-old who nearly fell for a fraud and reports it with his mother.

passage:
Saturday
There's a guy called Lokesh I've been gaming with for a month. He's older, maybe twenty. He's really good and he helps me level up.
Today he said, “Let's meet at the mall. Just us. Don't tell your parents, they won't understand.”
That line made my stomach go weird. Why would it be a secret?
I logged off without answering. I sat on my bed for a while. Then I went and showed Papa the chat.
He read it twice. He didn't shout. He said, “You did exactly the right thing, Tarun.” We blocked and reported Lokesh together, and Papa called the local police station's cyber cell to let them know.
I feel a bit sad. He was fun. But I'm glad I told. — Tarun

qa.q: Where did Lokesh want to meet?
qa.a: At the mall.

qa.q: How did Tarun feel when Lokesh asked for a secret meeting?
qa.a: Tarun felt uneasy, with a weird feeling in the stomach, sensing something was wrong.

qa.q: Why was showing Papa the right choice?
qa.a: It ended the contact safely and brought in a trusted adult who could block, report and inform the police.

qa.q: How did Papa react to the chat?
qa.a: He stayed calm, praised Tarun and acted the same day to block, report and call the cyber cell.

grounding: A fourteen-year-old recognises a grooming attempt and tells Papa, who acts the same day.

passage:
In the village, Kavitha's father got an SMS: "Congratulations! You have won Rs 25 lakh in the lucky draw. Pay Rs 5,000 processing fee to claim."
He was excited. "Kavitha, how do I send this money?"
Kavitha read it twice. Her friend Zainab, sitting with her, shook her head. "Uncle, we didn't enter any lucky draw."
"But it has a government logo!"
"Anyone can copy a logo," said Kavitha. "Real prizes don't ask you to pay first."
Her father looked at the phone, disappointed. "So it's a trick?"
"It's a scam. They want the fee."
Kavitha helped him block the number and report it on the national cyber crime helpline, 1930. Zainab told her own parents the same day. Two neighbours had got the same message.

qa.q: How much processing fee did the SMS ask for?
What was Kavitha's father feeling when he learned it was a scam?
qa.a: He felt disappointed and a bit embarrassed at nearly falling for it.

qa.q: What clues helped Kavitha and Zainab spot the scam?
qa.a: They hadn't entered any draw, and a real prize wouldn't ask for payment first; a copied logo proves nothing.

qa.q: How might the neighbours who got the same message be affected by Zainab telling her parents?
qa.a: They might be warned in time and avoid paying the fee, because word spread the same day.

grounding: A teen spots a lottery scam targeting her father and reports it.

passage:
In Oslo, Ingrid got a message from an unknown account: a photo of her face, edited onto someone else's body. "Send 500 kroner in gift cards or I post this everywhere."
Her hands went cold. It wasn't even her. But who would believe that?
She showed Rania at lunch. Rania said, "Don't pay. They'll just ask for more. Tell someone today."
Ingrid wanted to hide it. But after school she showed her mother.
Her mother read it, then held her. "It's not your fault. We're not paying." They saved screenshots, didn't reply, and reported it to the police online that evening. The next day they told the school.
Ingrid slept badly that night. But she wasn't alone with it.

qa.q: What did the message demand?
qa.a: 500 kroner in gift cards.

qa.q: What was Ingrid feeling when her hands went cold?
qa.a: Ingrid felt terrified and helpless, afraid people would believe the fake photo.

qa.q: Which steps kept Ingrid safer?
qa.a: Not paying, keeping screenshots, not replying, telling her mother the same day, and reporting to the police and school.

qa.q: How does Rania see the threat?
qa.a: Rania sees paying as a trap that leads to more demands and urges Ingrid to tell an adult right away.

grounding: A teen in Norway faces a blackmail attempt, refuses to pay and reports it the same day.

passage:
During the hostel's evening computer hour, Hrithik got a message on the class email: "Congratulations! You've won a new phone. Pay a small delivery fee and enter your bank OTP to claim." There was a countdown: 15 minutes left.
Hrithik was already reaching for his father's bank details on a note in his wallet. "It's from a real company, look at the logo."
Vijay leaned over. "Why would a free phone need an OTP? And the email address is a mix of numbers."
Hrithik hesitated. "But the timer…"
"The timer is the trick. So you don't think."
They took it to Mr Pinto, the lab in-charge, before doing anything. He checked it, said it was a scam, reported it to the school's IT team that evening and warned the whole hostel at dinner. He also called Hrithik's father, who hid the card details safely.

qa.q: What did the message ask Hrithik to enter to claim the phone?
qa.a: It asked him to pay a small delivery fee and enter his bank OTP.

qa.q: What was Hrithik feeling when he reached for the bank details?
qa.a: Hrithik felt excited and rushed by the countdown, and trusted the logo.

qa.q: Which clues did Vijay spot, and why is taking it to an adult the right step?
qa.a: Vijay spotted that a free phone doesn't need an OTP, and the odd email address; an adult could confirm the scam and report it quickly.

qa.q: How might Hrithik's father feel when Mr Pinto calls?
qa.a: His father might feel shaken that the card details were nearly shared, but relieved and grateful the boys asked for help first.

grounding: Shows teens recognising a fraud message's pressure tactics and reporting it to a trusted adult.

passage:
Dear Jaya Chechi,
Remember when you told me that anyone online who asks you to keep secrets is not a friend? I need to tell you that it helped.
There was a guy in my online game who said he was sixteen. He gave me free items for weeks. Then he started asking for photos, and said, "Don't tell your parents, they won't get it." My stomach went cold when I read that. It was exactly what you said.
I didn't reply. I took screenshots, blocked him, and went to Appa straight away, even though it was late. He didn't get angry. He said I did the right thing, sat with me while we reported the account to the game, and filled in the cyber crime report online that same night. This morning he told my class teacher too.
I feel stupid for trusting him. Appa says I shouldn't.
Jomon

qa.q: What did the player say when asking for photos?
qa.a: He said, "Don't tell your parents, they won't get it."

qa.q: How did Jomon feel on reading the request for secrecy?
qa.a: Jomon felt a cold jolt of fear, recognising the warning sign Jaya Chechi had described.

qa.q: What did Jomon do that others could follow?
qa.a: Jomon didn't reply, took screenshots, blocked the account and told a trusted adult straight away, who reported it that night.

qa.q: How might Appa have felt when Jomon came to him late at night?
qa.a: Appa was probably alarmed but proud and relieved that Jomon told him, which is why he stayed calm and acted at once. 🤍

grounding: Illustrates a teen recognising grooming tactics, ending contact and telling a parent who reports it the same night.

passage:
You asked how I dealt with it, so I'll say it straight. My name's Ramesh. Last year, someone I'd chatted with on a forum sent me an edited photo, my face stuck on something awful, and said, "Pay, or I send this to your whole school."
I couldn't breathe properly. I thought about paying. I thought about disappearing.
Instead I called my uncle Shankar. He's the one who never shouts. He came over that same hour. First thing he said: "This is not your fault, and you are not paying anyone." We didn't reply to the message. We saved everything, blocked the account and filed a complaint on the national cyber crime portal. The next morning he came with me to my principal.
The photo never went out. Maybe it would have, maybe not. But telling someone that day made it stop being mine to carry alone.

qa.q: What did Uncle Shankar say first?
qa.a: "This is not your fault, and you are not paying anyone."

qa.q: What was Ramesh feeling when the threat arrived?
qa.a: Ramesh felt terrified and trapped, struggling to breathe and thinking about paying or disappearing.

qa.q: Which steps did Ramesh and Shankar take, and why do they matter?
qa.a: They didn't reply, saved the evidence, blocked the account, reported it to the cyber crime portal and told the principal, so the blackmailer lost power and adults could act.

qa.q: How might Uncle Shankar have felt when Ramesh called him?
qa.a: Shankar was probably worried and angry at the blackmailer, but calm on the outside so Ramesh would feel safe.

grounding: Shows a teen facing a blackmail attempt, telling a trusted adult the same day and reporting it.

passage:
I'm Uday, Ishita's older brother. Last month I noticed she'd stopped eating properly and jumped every time her phone buzzed.
One night she came to my room, shaking, and showed me her messages. Someone she'd met in a game, who said he was sixteen, had got a photo of her face and made it into a fake picture. Now he was saying, "Send more or I share this with your school. Don't tell anyone."
I told her, "This isn't your fault. You did right by showing me." We woke Mummy and Papa right then. Papa took screenshots, and they reported the account on the cybercrime portal that night. Next morning they went to the police station and told her class teacher, just in case.
She blocked him and hasn't replied since. I don't know everything she felt, but she slept in Mummy's room for a week, and slowly started laughing again.

qa.q: What did the person threaten to do?
qa.a: He said he would share the fake picture with her school.

qa.q: What was Ishita likely feeling before she showed Uday the messages?
qa.a: She was likely terrified and ashamed, jumping every time her phone buzzed and not eating properly.

qa.q: Which choice protected Ishita best, and why?
qa.a: Telling her brother, who woke their parents that same night to save evidence and report it, because trusted adults could stop the blackmail and she didn't face it alone.

qa.q: How does Uday respond to seeing his sister in this situation?
qa.a: Uday stays calm and protective, telling her it isn't her fault and bringing in their parents straight away.

grounding: Shows a teenager recognising online blackmail, ending contact and getting trusted adults to report it the same night.
